HiPICO matches state-of-the-art hand tracking methods while performing significantly better than current state-of-the-art object-based methods, with source code publicly available for review.

This study employs the modular reduction technique to a Coxeter group of rank four featuring a star diagram with five or six edges. Using this method, we establish the existence of a specific noncrystallographic complex reflection group of rank four, along with its corresponding Christol number, which matches the interleaving number of the group's ordered reflection length sequence with that of a related finite Coxeter group.

A novel markerless system has been developed to easily configure and calibrate a depth camera on a robotic system for various tasks. The system employs machine learning to accurately determine the position and orientation of the end-effector from a depth image, allowing for a quicker and less dependent process to set up a robotic system for performing pick and place operations. The effectiveness of this system has been demonstrated in a practical scenario where a PEC10 robotic arm and a ZCAM EYE depth camera were used to set up a setup-independent protocol that can be applied to other robotic systems with similar specifications. The results show significant time savings and reliability in determining the end-effector pose from depth images, allowing the robotic system to successfully perform tasks in a bin-picking setup.

A new model is introduced to describe therapy interference in observational studies, where k nearest neighboring units are affected by an treated unit's values. Under this model, we develop tests to assess interference in linear regression models with various error distributions, using both fixed and dependent sample sizes. For both cases, our tests have optimal asymptotic power and maintain consistency as specified sample sizes approach infinity. Since establishing exact critical values is challenging, we devise an alternative method involving bootstrap approximations. Through simulations, our approach is shown to perform well, even with limited data, and is applied to an actual study on gestational diabetes therapy.

Calculations of neutrino emissions from self-interacting Dark Matter within Neutron Stars are being investigated, with a focus on the influence of a specific scalar mediator. As a Neutron Star's density decreases with distance from its core, it's believed that only lower energy states can traverse the core, while higher energy states are confined there. This density gradient may facilitate Dark Matter annihilation reactions near the surface, despite the core being fully immersed in the Dark Matter field. A major consideration in these processes is the presence of a gamma-ray signal that can be detected with greater sensitivity than neutrinos, primarily because a stronger electromagnetic field near the surface enhances detectable gamma-ray signals while neutrinos are poorly detected. To refine estimates of neutrino emissions, we update existing cross-sections with the latest mediator models, also developing a new numerical algorithm for neutrino emissions. A numerical analysis indicates that even with a relatively low Dark Matter mass (less than 100 GeV) and relatively short reaction ranges, a significant surface signal can still be detected, with a large influence of electromagnetic interactions near the surface dominating the process.

The ongoing UNIONS project, the most comprehensive optical survey in the Canadian Forking Intermediate Small camera net, has provided 6450 deg^2 of area with minimal distortion and high resolution. With the release of shape information becoming increasingly essential for future galaxy surveys, we introduce ShapePipe, a highly versatile and efficient software that employs ngmix to analyze single images and calculates average shapes for small regions. With the aid of ShapePipe, we analyzed the UNIONS/CFIS data to produce the very first large-scale galaxy shape catalog with low systematic error, yielding more than 132,000 deg^2 with 20,000 regions of high resolution. By employing the cosmology-Independent Method for Reconstruction of Inflationary Parameters, model fits indicate a linear mass-to-light ratio ratio of 280 ± 20 solar masses/((h 70)^2) with the dark energy parameter space narrowed down to a rectangular area. With the data, we discovered that second order quadrupole and octupole moments provide insightful information on galaxy shapes, featuring naturally aligned directions not solely due to E/B mode separation.

Building upon the work of Kronecker and Weyl, our research in this paper delves into generalizing the initial result. The new findings regarding the equidistribution of points generated by irrationals, as well as lattices in real and complex spaces, are significant. We demonstrate the application of a novel change of variables to the original K-W result, yielding a generalization that covers the entire parameter space. To accomplish this, we leverage a specific formula, for which we establish the validity. In the process, we revisit the original K-W proof and incorporate additional concepts to explore equidistribution over specific manifolds. The generalization of the K-W result initiates an inquiry into the diophantine approximation of specific numbers, as well as geodesic lines in real and complex spaces, generating new questions and outcomes.

We prove that a d-dimensional local complete intersection variety is k-rational if it meets certain conditions, such as being defined by polynomials of codimension d in k-x space. This allows us to conclude that a k-Du Bois variety satisfying these conditions is indeed k-rational. The reasoning behind this involves showing that the top local cohomology module with support in the exceptional set of the minimal resolution is 0.

We've observed the Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) transition in the spin-exchange model on a two-dimensional lattice with a simple Heisenberg magnet, where the BKT transition is not directly visible due to the lack of experimental data, but its effects are evident in our findings. In a three-dimensional lattice, our research shows that the chiral order parameter exhibits slow decay over short distances and non-linear power-law behavior over longer distances. We apply renormalization group analysis to the 2D and 3D spin models and find that their behavior can be accurately described by the Gaussian model, resulting in consistent predictions with our numerical data. By applying an external magnetic field with various orientations, our research also explores the resistance variation in quantum Hall systems and provides insights into the characteristics of chiral Lattice Chirality in quantum Hall phases.

We introduce a theoretical framework called Shadow Matter Theory, which proposes an additional neutrino type that doesn't participate in the standard model. By masking the invisible decay of neutrinos into these shadow neutrinos, we can account for non-zero mixing angles between regular and shadow neutrinos. Using data from the large underground German experiment MEPhI, we set a new limit on the axion-electron coupling with a minimum of $4.5 \times 10^{-5}$, and discuss the potential of exploring additional parameter spaces with future experiments.

This study optimizes the quantum resource usage of the variational quantum eigensolver method, a widely recognized quantum algorithm for simulators and computers. The efficiency of this method is directly tied to the distance between a given magic state and the nearest stabilizer state. Previous research established an upper limit on the distance between a magic state and the nearest stabilizer state in terms of logarithmic factors. This paper refines those findings, eliminating the log factor and providing a more precise benchmark. Additionally, a similar analysis is performed for the Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) state and the multi-qubit Clifford phase is investigated. The new bounds are applied to estimate the runtime of the variational quantum eigensolver, leading to significant improvements in 3-qubit GHZ state calculations.

This research employs the Essence model to describe the evolution of universe equations, where we substitute Tsallis holographic dark energy into the model and perform a parameter analysis. The model is initially presented, followed by derivations of field equations and energy density conditions for Tsallis energy density, after which we determine crucial parameters by performing best-fit analyses using SnIa data, shift space data, Hubble volume data, planck data and CFRS data.

Between October 2019 and April 2020, the LAMOST performed a unique observational study using four $K$2 plates. This study, which involved low- and medium-resolution spectroscopic surveys, gathered a significant amount of data. The low-resolution spectroscopic survey yielded around 767,000 spectra after 25 nights of 46.6 hours of exposures and a low signal-to-noise ratio higher than 10 for about 70% of its spectra. The medium-resolution spectroscopic survey took 177 exposures and around 49.1 hours over 27 nights to collect around 478,000 spectra with a low signal-to-noise ratio higher than 10. This early time-domain research yielded data on numerous moving objects such as 30161 DD, 35179 and 35179D, as well as others. It also gathered data on PTF1J050649.13+370948.3 which is believed to be an APG. The LAMOST time-domain research is now continuously conducting low- and medium-resolution spectroscopic surveys of a changing sky. This particular study served as a launch pad for a broader endeavor.

Recent research has been focusing on enhancing TRNGs, which are integral to dependable computing systems, by utilizing diverse physical phenomena. Unlike existing solutions that rely on specialized hardware or digital approximations, this work introduces a novel technique that generates high-quality random numbers, which are then utilized to prevent SRAM data corruption and ensure CPU stability in uncertain environments. Experiments have been conducted using a Silver Armour-based evaluation platform, which has revealed the feasibility and efficiency of the proposed method in utilizing SRAM's inherent variability for random number generation. The study demonstrates that the generated random numbers adhere to high standards, exceeding the requirements set by various industry standards, including NIST, ANSI, and ISO. Furthermore, this work highlights the practical applications of randomness-based techniques in mitigating memory corruption and ensuring CPU stability, which can be particularly useful in uncertain environments in the aerospace and medical sectors.

A theoretical model of a single-electron resistor that acts like a nonvolatile memory device has been developed. It consists of two parts: a Coulomb blockade region, which controls the flow of charge, and a highly conductive gate connected to a external voltage source. The conductive gate acts as a electrode that can exchange electrons with the system. When the external voltage allows the exchange of electrons, the device enters a state of quasi-equilibrium. The proposed model was tested using two different molecular structures, and simulations showed that the characteristics of these devices can be controlled through tuning of the length of the molecular link. The results of these calculations are presented in a study published in the journal ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces.

A novel approach called LoopSkyrme, a numerical and graphical evaluation technique, is introduced to efficiently evaluate multi-loop Feynman integrals, enabling the creation of pictorial representations of integrals through a series of simple, topological graphs called causal skrymes. By breaking down complex integrals into a set of fundamental loop structures, called causal blocks, and evaluating them separately, the full integral can be computed with high precision. This framework has several key benefits: it easily adapts to different gauge theories and is not heavily dependent on space-time dimensions, making it a versatile tool for a wide range of applications. Additionally, the underlying physics problem is translated into a combinatorial challenge, involving the combination of graphs consisting of lines with specific properties, rendering the evaluation semi-numerical and largely computation-free. This framework can be employed in the study of particle physics at various scales, including those probed by the LHC and future collider projects, as well as in the analysis of physical phenomena affecting the behavior of particles in external fields and the properties of particles themselves.

This paper proves that a specific real number k is related to the eigenvalues of the one-dimensional two-state quantum walk by the equation sin(√k^2t)^2 = cos(√k^2t)^2 + sin(√k^2t)^2. To solve this equation, we first show that the desired values of k are linked to the frequencies ω in the equation cos(ωt) = e^(i*ω*t). By rearranging this equation, we arrive at the desired eigenvalue problem, and the desired values of k are shown to be connected to the eigenvalues of a symmetric tridiagonal matrix with specific entries. Having found a relationship between k and the eigenvalues of this matrix, we show that the corresponding eigenfunctions of this matrix provide a complete set of orthogonal functions which can expand the wave function of the one-dimensional two-state quantum walk. Our analysis shows that this wave function can be expressed as the product of the eigenvalues of this matrix and the corresponding eigenfunctions of this matrix.

This study examines the composition of hybrid stars formed by neutrons, protons, and various other particles. The analysis combines the Sigma-omega-rho theory, governing certain nuclear interactions, with two distinct matter models: the MIT bag model and the NJL model. By calculating mass thresholds and using two different equations relating pressure and density, various models are created to predict hybrid star properties, such as mass and radius. These models are then evaluated against observed stellar masses, with considerations for implications on understanding hadronic matter and the behavior of quark confinement within these stars.

We investigate the behavior of light as it passes through a q-deformed optomechanical system. When the mechanical part of the system is in its initial state, our analysis shows that the transmission pattern of light is affected by changes in the q-deformation parameter and the Poincaré parameter. As the mechanical part transitions energetically, the transmission pattern of light undergoes significant changes, including the formation of multiple transmission bands. Moreover, we find that the system can amplify light optically. To better understand these phenomena, we use plots to demonstrate how the system's transmission properties and optical enhancement change based on the q-deformation parameter and the Poincaré parameter.

In a model where nucleons and quarks have different rotational properties, there's a unique phenomenon where a nucleus's rotational levels can rapidly decouple, leading to contrasting properties. Investigating this effect within a nucleus's structure, it's possible to understand the adverse R-parity segregation phenomenon, a concept recently introduced. Taking the $0-0$ $\gamma$ transition in $^{180}$W as a case study, it's shown that the underlying structure's characteristics, specifically how rotational levels are arranged, can influence the transition's intensity. Additionally, it's suggested that this same model can help clarify the absence of certain transitions in other nuclei as well.

The properties of thin films made from metallic transition-metal oxides can be significantly different from their bulk counterparts. In this discussion, the possible origins of spin and orbital disordering in these films are explored. The examples considered include titanium doped with vanadium in magnesium oxide, iron oxide with varying levels of iron, and vanadium oxide with different levels of vanadium doping. The interface between the metal and the oxygen ion cloud is suggested as a key factor influencing disordering. This interface can produce a significant amount of vibrational energy that can affect the spin and orbital alignment. Additionally, the strain caused by the mismatch in lattice size between the metal and the oxide can impact the spin and orbital structure. This strain can also produce new energy levels that may influence the spin and orbital behavior. The examples considered demonstrate the significant impact that electron filling has on spin and orbital alignment and the resulting magnetic properties.

Recent research on optical lattices has revealed that cold-atom systems can be modelled using the hopping qubit model, a quantum circuit that mimics the behavior of quantum spins. This model is particularly notable because it leads to a quantum phase transition despite the absence of long-range interactions. In a recent study, researchers cooled rubidium atoms using a laser trap and then analyzed their behavior as it escaped from a trap that fluctuated in strength. This analysis revealed unusual patterns in the system's energy distribution, its correlation structure, and the occurrence of rare events. Notably, the system's 1d behavior converged slowly to that of 2d ergodicity, with its local properties diverging from global properties. The researchers also discovered that the system's local properties followed a symmetric pattern, with its global properties deviating from this symmetry. These findings are significant because they demonstrate the emergence of dissipative invariants in an open quantum system.

Cryptocurrencies have thrived on decentralized networks, enabling individuals to buy, sell, and exchange digital currencies. Our research examines the interconnections among cryptocurrency traders based on transaction data. By employing a weighted network analysis, we identify the structural properties of the network and assess how cryptocurrency values are affected by the connections between traders. Our findings reveal that the shaping of cryptocurrency prices is attributed to the pair-wise and higher-order relationships among traders, and a significant portion of this influence arises from the largest trader groups. Furthermore, we determine that the trading strategies of prominent groups correlate with market trends, and their activities result in significant profits. By refining their strategies, these leading traders can yield greater profits, and their modified approaches also yield better outcomes for lesser-known groups, thereby potentially driving market trends.

The formation of particles from trace gases is a crucial source of cloud condensation nuclei that facilitate the creation of clouds due to their rapid growth mechanisms. The role of vibrational motion in these processes is frequently neglected, but it may be equally important to classical motion in certain scenarios. We carried out a study using the statistical rate theory to examine the role of vibrational motion in the recombination of hydrogens and oxygen from water and sulphuric acid. Our results show that incorporating zero-point motion significantly increases the reaction rates by at least 5 times. This substantial boost in reaction rates has major implications for new particle formation predictions, suggesting that quantum effects cannot be disregarded in such processes. Furthermore, the present study's findings shed light on the importance of utilizing anharmonic and high-precision potential energy surfaces in modeling particle formation through quantum mechanics.

We establish the definitions for a compact perception pair, compactifying a perception pair, and compactifying a space of operators invariant under group actions, specifically focusing on the case where these actions are linear and represented by matrices. It's demonstrated that for a perception pair $(X, \Phi)$, if $X$ is compact and $\Phi$ is a continuous mapping from a compact space, then $(X, \Phi)$ is a compact perception pair. Additionally, it's shown that a perception pair $(X, \Phi)$ can be transformed into a compact perception pair $(X', \Phi')$ through a process of embedding and equivariant contraction, where $X'$ is the result of embedding $X$ into a compact space, and $\Phi'$ is the consequence of contracting $\Phi$ while maintaining group invariance. It's established that the space of compact, non-expanding operators invariant under group actions is closed and forms a Fréchet manifold. Similarly, it's shown that the space of compact, bounded non-expanding operators invariant under group actions is compact and satisfies the conditions of a Fréchet Banach space. These findings build upon earlier research by Boudaaf, Boulmezaa, and El Karroumi.

A novel reaction is observed, where a thermal Hall effect is generated not by chiral modes, but through a normal mode interacting with a thermal bath. This reaction mimics the thermal expansion of an ideal gas, yet contradicts predictions based on an analogy between gravity and electronics. Additionally, the Einstein relations and specific heat capacity laws are violated. This phenomenon can be realized using coupled systems of superconducting cavities with leaky interfaces.

In various machine learning tasks, overparameterized neural networks consistently achieve impressive outcomes, despite exceeding the minimum requirement for model capacity. Our research explores how network simplicity is influenced by geometric constraints imposed by differential geometry. We demonstrate that many of these geometric regulators, such as curvature restrictions and Ricci curvature, simplify neural networks. Furthermore, the geometric perspective offers a unified understanding of various complexity regulators, such as Lipschitz regularization, as well as the effect of batch normalization, which we also investigate.

A study involving a semileptonic decay of $B^0$ to $K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ is carried out to establish the $K^{*0}$ meson's polarization in this process. This investigation uses data collected from an integrated luminosity of 5.8 fb$^{-1}$ of $e^+e^-\to \rho^+\rho^-$ collisions at an energy of 10.58 GeV, where the $K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ candidate events are identified through a 4D likelihood fit incorporating decay shape analysis. Ultimately, this study estimates the Wilson coefficients $c_9$ and $c_{10}$ in the Standard Model and finds their first-order correlation with each other. Additionally, this study includes a comparison with the current best-fit results from other $b\to s\mu^+\mu^-$ analyses and the latest theoretical predictions with or without new physics contributions.

The cost-effectiveness of automated essay grading depends on its ability to achieve low error rates, which poses a significant challenge, particularly when dealing with extended writing samples. Recent advancements in transformer-based models have led to improved performance, but training them necessitates substantial data augmentation to bypass the limitations of small datasets. Our investigation explores data enhancement techniques for employing transformer models in automated essay grading. Specifically, we examine how different augmentation methods, including sentence duplication, sentence shuffling, and sentence insertion, affect their performance. Our findings indicate that, when paired with multi-task learning, these techniques can significantly boost the accuracy of automated essay grading using BERT and ALBERT models.

A new type of copula-based model is introduced, where a multivariate probability distribution is constructed using individual "marginal dependence models" that incorporate local copulas, enabling the analysis of local dependence in statistical models. We demonstrate the usefulness of this method through an examination of a local dependence model in a multivariate extreme value context and a Bayesian approach to modeling multivariate data. The use of marginal dependence models also enables the identification and estimation of interest rates based on bond prices, facilitating a more comprehensive understanding of dependence in financial markets.

We've developed a simple theoretical model of social mobility that occurs across multiple generations to better understand how economic opportunities are passed down through the generations. In this model, individuals are classified into groups with varying levels of income, and the likelihood of intergingeneration social mobility depends on the level of income. Over time, the distribution of social mobility opportunities changes and can be represented by the probability of moving to a higher income group given a parent's income level. Our model also considers situations where social mobility is limited to staying within or moving to a higher income group. By applying our model to data from the United States, Canada, and Britain, we've found support for a simple rule that describes how the distribution of social mobility opportunities changes as income levels increase.

The relationship between spin and statistics, traditionally based on how particles rotate, is reevaluated using a symmetry principle. By considering a particle with no momentum as a symmetric object, the allowed symmetries of the wavefunction are examined, leading to a derivation of the Pauli statistical factor through analysis of the single-particle Schrödinger equation. This approach does not rely on relativistic ideas.

We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that supports stealth addresses in conjunction with Delegated Proof of Stake, resulting in the Delegated RingCT protocol. The Delegated RingCT protocol is adaptable to various dPoS-based cryptocurrencies. Our work focuses on improving the financial privacy of these cryptocurrencies by mitigating address visible transactions. To this end, we describe an efficient Delegated RingCT implementation for Zelcash, a cryptocurrency that previously incorporated RingCT.

Our Delegated RingCT implementation features two key components: 

1. A comprehensive collection of transparent public keys that encompass all possible public key values, used to create an expanded basis of encodable values. 
2. A customized RingCT transaction format, incorporating modified $k$-way RingCT transactions, along with an optimized transaction structure for even distribution of public key values.

We also discuss an alternative Delegated RingCT implementation that relies on a subset of public keys, specifically those listed on the Zelcash roadmap, with the aim of reducing computation time during the encoding process.

The stability of solvers for linear systems in the face of arbitrary column permutations is a key area of focus for this work. Given that any finite-dimensional system has a bounded number of columns, we understand the theoretical limits of solvers that use space, specifically when dealing with systems whose Schur complement has an inherent rank deficiency. By building upon this foundation, we derive sequential and block algorithms that efficiently tackle multiple right-hand sides for various system variants, including triangular and Hermitian triangular. These algorithms not only offer reduced space complexity but also serve as minimal memory-footprint implementations, necessitating no prior factorization and only utilizing the system matrix to the extent of its triangular parts. Finally, we examine the implications of our theoretical results on the design of memory-efficient linear system solvers and illustrate their utility with several device-level simulation problems.

The production rates of three bosons at 13 TeV are examined, considering production modes such as $t$ channel and others. Calculations are carried out using next-to-leading order perturbation theory, incorporating corrections beyond tree level in QCD and electroweak interactions. Studies reveal significant contributions from the top-quark loop in WZW production and also point out discrepancies between measured and predicted values for this process. Furthermore, findings suggest that most QCD-based production mechanisms of WWZ and ZZZ are overestimated when using tree-level approximations, highlighting the necessity of employing higher-order perturbative corrections in these calculations. Total production cross-sections for these processes are estimated to be around 0.4-0.5 fb. It's also noted that spontaneous neutrino production in high-energy proton-proton collisions is impractically challenging due to the absence of neutrino masses and associated feasibility issues.

Previous efforts to create an UD treebank for Hebrew were hindered by the difficulties of processing its complex script and language patterns, as well as a lack of research assistance. A revised dataset, ud-he, has been developed using a Forced Alignment tool to match Hebrew texts with UD annotations. This new dataset addresses issues from the earlier attempt and significantly updates the previous results. In the context of Hebrew, which is often written in a different script from its computer representation, specific challenges arise, including the handling of titles and footnotes in news articles and biblical texts. A critical evaluation of the current state of Hebrew UD treebanks is also presented, accompanied by experiments in parsing tasks using the SAMSA platform. To boost performance, the Hebrew UD treebanks have been augmented with additional information from aligned sources, including Israel Radio broadcasts and the Bible. This new augmentation brings significant improvements in parsing accuracy for Hebrew and Yiddish, which is written in the same script as Hebrew. Hebrew UD treebanks now show results on a par with those of European languages in the CoLA evaluations.

We establish that for any fixed $1 < p < \infty$ and $\varepsilon > 0$, a linear map from $\ell_p$ to $\ell_q$ with $1 < p < q < \infty$ or $\infty < p < q < \infty$ is said to be $\varepsilon$-isometric if it satisfies a specific criterion related to the inclusion of its image of $\ell_s$ within $\ell_q$, where $1 \leq s < p$. The rule states that the dimension of the space on the left should be less than or equal to a specific constant multiplied by the dimension of the space on the right, where the constant depends on $\varepsilon$. This research includes specific results for $\ell_p$ and $c_0$ spaces as well as for directed spaces like $\ell_s$ and $c_{0,1}$.

The explosion of data from many fields has sparked an urgent need for theories and algorithms that can handle numerous variables and lack of domain-specific knowledge. We've developed a new approach to data-driven modeling by leveraging relationships between data sets. The core of this methodology involves introducing a concept of similarity between data sets, which can be applied to develop efficient algorithms for collaborative modeling. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through various applications, including multi-variable regression, dimensionality reduction, and image classification, achieved by fusing insights from multiple datasets.

The stability of arbitrary LDPC codes under binary deletion channel is examined and an analytical method for calculating the error probability of these codes is developed, specifically for codes defined by a parity-check matrix where degree distributions and the distribution of connections between codes and messages are predetermined. Additionally, a method for generating a parity-check matrix with specified degree distributions and a connection pattern is presented, and this framework is applied to determine the limiting error probability of various LDPC code families.

A novel adaptive robust linear control system is designed to protect an underlying system with unknown disturbances from both internal and external sources. The disturbance is expected to have a specific pattern, defined by a predictive security filter (PSF), which acts as a leading indicator facilitating the identification of controlling signals for the system. The PSF is developed using System Level Synthesis, enabling its optimization and application in the controller design. A dynamic output feedback controller is then designed, and its effectiveness is demonstrated in simulations.

A critical component in the development of post-quantum cryptography is the decoy-state quantum key distribution (QKD) protocol. Recently, a novel approach incorporating phase randomization (PR) and measurement settings has been introduced to enhance the efficiency of distilling keys in long-distance QKD networks. Specifically, this improved protocol employs the phase of signal states to be varied, whereas all other states maintain a fixed phase, thereby reducing the number of necessary measurement settings needed to achieve a predetermined key distillation efficiency. However, our research reveals that this optimized protocol is susceptible to a sophisticated form of attack devised by our team, which involves manipulating only the interferometric phase of the signal states while retaining the phases of other states. As a result, the predicted key distillation efficiency in the recommended PR protocol is significantly lower than the expected value, with our attack capable of yielding an unlimited amount of eavesdropted information. Conversely, our study also demonstrates that the virtual unbreakable QKD protocol, which uses distinct distribution of phases in signal states, is immune to this sophisticated form of attack and remains robust against various forms of quantum intrusion.

Recent studies on large language models have demonstrated in-context zero- and few-shot learning abilities with promising results, yet their underlying dynamics are not yet fully understood. For instance, there is limited knowledge about how learning in-context changes when using varying training corpora. Our investigation delves into the influence of a pretraining corpus's size, domain, and diversity on in-context learning. Specifically, we explored a pretraining corpus consisting of 48 domains, each represented by 10,000 texts, and discovered that a model can perform well on unseen tasks without any fine-tuning. Notably, the relationship between in-context learning performance and training corpus size follows an S-curve pattern, while a domain's influence is largely attributed to its similarity with the target task. Moreover, a model's capabilities in in-context learning can be enhanced by utilizing a training corpus with the most relevant domains, and our findings also show that a higher training corpus can sometimes hinder a model's performance in in-context learning.

Galaxy cluster observations have primarily focused on the formation of central filaments, neglecting the role of shearing forces that are significant in this process. Despite its minimal appearance in the X-ray spectrum, thermal energy plays a crucial role in the creation of a shearing flow that prevents filament collapse. A numerical model incorporating magnetic fields, thermal conduction, and cooling rates has been used to investigate the development of a cold cloud within a galaxy cluster. The analysis revealed that when a galaxy passes through a cluster, its trail forms a distinctive U-shape due to shearing forces, which are in turn affected by the balance of conduction and cooling. Notably, an increase in magnetic field strength leads to a U-shape centered on the galaxy's original path, while a rise in cooling rate causes the U-shape to shift forward and the vertex becomes sharper. Conversely, enhanced thermal conduction causes the vertex to move in the direction of the galaxy's current path, creating a longer, U-shaped cloud. If magnetic fields are eliminated, the cloud assumes a symmetrical, comet-like shape. The ratio of thermal to kinetic energy within the cloud is primarily determined by the balance between conduction and cooling, with a higher cooling rate resulting in a higher kinetic energy ratio, which in turn causes the cloud to disintegrate into multiple clouds along the galaxy's current path.

The discovery of CP violation in beauty mesons during the 2001 ICHEP conference by Francis Paulinchi was a significant one, marking the first observation of CP violation beyond its original dimensions in nature. The concept of beauty had been tied to the characteristics of CP symmetry, with the standard model able to explain the observed effect through changes in its matrix elements and the mass difference between the K and the $\pi$ particles. However, as the unitarity triangle of the CKM matrix is further examined, uncertainties remain, leaving room for additional beyond-the-standard-model physics to influence this phenomenon. Furthermore, as data on CP violation in beauty mesons continues to flow in from Belle, BaBar, CDF, and D0, among others, our understanding of this effect will become increasingly precise, likely allowing us to determine if these results align with the predictions of the standard model or hint at new physics.

New bosonic scattering amplitudes for chains of $n$ $D$-branes have been calculated in superstring theory, and their calculations were facilitated by a new representation of bosonic amplitudes. This involved expressing them through Chern-Simons forms on $D^n$-branes. The conjecture by Gross that the ratio of $D$-brane to $D$-anti-brane scattering amplitudes is constant has been verified for all chain lengths. Additionally, the rational dependence of the ratio of $D$-brane to $D$-anti-brane scattering amplitudes on the level of the $D$-brane has been theoretically confirmed.

With the increasing reliance on mobile connectivity, cellular networks are expected to handle the demands of a multitude of mobile applications, including those of massive IoT devices. To meet these requirements, next-generation cellular networks must employ efficient energy management to minimize their carbon footprint. To this end, this paper introduces a new framework that enables self-organizing cellular networks to optimize energy consumption while maintaining satisfactory user communication. The framework relies on a distributed voting system to facilitate decision-making at the network level, and a deep reinforcement learning approach is presented to develop an energy-efficient core network administration procedure. The results show that this new procedure leads to a significant reduction (up to 35%) in core network energy consumption without compromising users' quality of service.

The objective of zero-speech voice synthesis is to create a vocal version of text without the need for annotated speech data, which is extremely difficult under normal conditions. Recent studies have made significant breakthroughs by employing unsupervised transcript revision and speech unit density estimation to generate speech directly from text, but the process remains highly demanding in terms of computational power. Moreover, the quality of the resulting synthesis is still relatively low compared to state-of-the-art speech synthesis systems using extensive training data. In this study, we introduce an alternative approach that utilizes acoustic features derived directly from speech, which are then incorporated into a neural network for voice synthesis trained with self-supervised methods. The proposed approach is grounded in the idea that a broad frequency range is essential for effective speech synthesis. We also investigate the utilization of natural language processing (NLP) models to correct transcription errors and revise speech units, which are then fed into a speech synthesis model. Additionally, we introduce a metric to evaluate the rhytmic quality of the synthesized speech and conduct listening tests to assess the synthetic speech's intelligibility and its similarity to natural speech.

Real-time control of high-doF robots is challenging due to computational limitations in inner loops of control algorithms, but a feasible solution involves breaking down complex inner loop problems into simpler ones using McCormick envelope relaxations in coupled optimization frameworks. This approach is applied to a humanoid robot to reduce its joint velocity limit constraints, resulting in a significant reduction of up to 90% in computation time and an acceptable 2% error rate. Extensions to other problems, such as integrating forward dynamics models and optimizing multi-stage motion planning, show the potential for complete motion planning between two targets in as short as 30ms.

Engineer and material scientist Mark M. Wilde has identified and analyzed all possible ways to transform one quantum state into another, and the resulting collection of techniques is known as the family of techniques for probabilistic convertibility.  The techniques for achieving this transformation vary depending on the specific scenario:  sometimes, a perfect copy of the original state is extracted with certainty, while in other cases, the desired state is obtained with a certain probability.  By leveraging a quantitative measure called the hyperconvexity of a set, Wilde demonstrated that a particular class of quantum states, known as maximal completely entangling inequalities (MCEIs), play a pivotal role in determining the techniques for probabilistic convertibility.  Notably, Wilde showed that the MCEIs are the smallest set of techniques necessary for achieving the probabilistic transformation, and he further refined this understanding by identifying a different class of quantum states, known as minimal universal completely entangling inequalities (MUCEIs), whose existence is essential for implementing the techniques of probabilistic transformability.  By combining these new findings with previously established results by Pomeransky et al. that relate MUCEIs to stochastic equality under the action of a quantum map, Wilde was able to determine the precise extent to which MUCEIs remain unchanged under the action of a quantum map, and he connected this question to an open problem in quantum information theory concerning the relationship between MUCEIs and total quantum maps. We investigated the dynamic behavior of a cup of coffee being placed in a vehicle that experiences a series of sudden decelerations. These shocks cause the coffee to oscillate like a pendulum, and through both experimental and numerical approaches, we identified four distinct modes of motion. The most intriguing mode, which has garnered significant attention in recent years, is just one of many dynamics at play in this situation.

In our research, we address the challenge of jointly learning multiple tasks in a network where data is stored at the nodes and interconnected in a graph structure. Due to the high communication cost and interdependence of tasks, decentralized training is necessary but faces obstacles from biased gradient estimates and limited communication opportunities. To overcome these hurdles, we develop a new algorithm called DR-DSGD, which is inspired by the theory of distributionally robust learning and utilizes an entropy-bounded regularizer to compensate for data class imbalances in the network. By rigorously proving its convergence and experimental verification on synthetic and real-world data, we demonstrate that DR-DSGD is a reliable and efficient method for multi-task decentralized training.

We utilize the concept of hydrodynamic attractors to establish a universal relationship between initial energy states and the number of produced particles in high-energy nuclear collisions. By combining this new approach with an in-depth analysis of the longitudinal and transverse fluctuations observed in relativistic nuclear collisions, we develop a unified framework to quantify the energy released and particle production in these events. Our research reveals that the energy released and particle production in peripheral collisions can be predicted using a single universal function, thereby reducing variability and uncertainty associated with non-equilibrium initial conditions. Additionally, our study shows that the majority of produced particles arise from the energy released by the initial state, both globally and locally.

Using complex simulations of star-forming clouds, the process by which powerful jets form is studied under different magnetic field strengths and mass accumulation rates. The data show that strongly magnetized clouds produce fast-moving jets only when the protostar gains a relatively low mass each year, around 2 × 10^-4 M_⊙. However, in cases where the protostar grows more rapidly, the jets become slower, ultimately merging with wider outflow systems. It's observed that magnetization in clouds plays a crucial role in determining both the velocity and volume of outflow produced, with a higher magnetic strength resulting in greater outflow and accelerated outflow motion. The laboratory testing of this process mimics real-life star formation through a flow past a solid sphere in a laboratory setting.

This study tackles the issue of optimal control for nonlinear systems with limitations, where a new approach has demonstrated improved performance in a variety of test cases, including numerous heat transfer systems with significant thermal masses. Compared to the standard Euler method, the Lddim method offers several benefits, such as reduced discretization errors, faster convergence, and better capture of system transients. However, its application in nonlinear systems with limitations is complicated by an ill-posed problem that arises from discretization, which must be mitigated in order to achieve accurate solutions. Building on the Lddim method's success, a new algorithm, referred to as Lddim-Con, has been developed to address the optimality conditions resulting from the Euler-Lagrange equations of these systems. This novel method has successfully overcome the challenges posed by system limitations, resulting in a precise solution that matches the Euler-Lagrange equations' stationary points. A comprehensive examination of the Lddim-Con method's capabilities is provided by applying it to multiple single heat transfer unit examples, which show that it outperforms prior methods in terms of accuracy, while also demonstrating its ability to model system nonlinearities effectively. Furthermore, a multi-body system consisting of several interconnected heat transfer units has been successfully analyzed using the Lddim-Con method, which confirmed its capability to capture complex system transients. As a result, the Lddim-Con method is an invaluable tool for optimizing the performance of constrained nonlinear systems, providing a precise and efficient solution that cannot be

This research investigates the solar radiation pressure impact on small celestial bodies, specifically how it induces periodic variations in their orbital periods, and the implications for their equilibrium positions. The study initially examines the influence of solar pressure on the 1/2 resonant system, followed by an extension to general, integer resonant systems. Both theoretical and numerical approaches are used to explore the effects of solar pressure, focusing on establishing criteria for identifying equilibrium positions in these systems. Numerical simulations are conducted to validate the theoretical findings and predict various orbital configurations that can emerge under the influence of solar pressure.

We synthesize the approaches of wave-particle duality and relativity to derive a general framework for quantizing any physical model that exhibits symmetry and can be expressed mathematically. We apply this formalism to a type of model used to study electronic behavior, converting them into quantum systems that preserve conservation laws. Our method is tested on a range of tight-binding models, including those with interacting electrons, and we demonstrate that these models retain the properties of their parent physical systems.

Our proposed approach for PCL (Perception and Control for Lifting) aims to identify the pose and shape of objects within a specific category by utilizing semantic keypoints extracted from 2D and 3D images or point clouds. PCL leverages category-models, training them to recognize relevant characteristics and perform essential calculations in a pre-processing stage, allowing for real-time operations. By optimizing object recognition through a combination of accurate pose estimation and shape assessment, PCL generates robust results even in challenging scenarios. PCL is applied to various tasks including object classification, pose estimation, and shape analysis, and demonstrates exceptional performance across diverse datasets for object categorization (PASCAL, ImageNet, COCO), as well as pose estimation and shape analysis (Linemod, TAG, OCRCloud). Our research reveals that PCL's training data and results are notably resilient to glints, occlusions, and pose-driven transformations.

This research establishes equations for calculating confidence intervals and squares at a specified confidence level for parameters in Cauchy distributions, using maximum likelihood estimations and asymptotic properties. Specifically, it employs the chi-square distribution with degrees of freedom based on the sample size to construct intervals and squares, which are validated through simulations. The study also investigates the bias in estimators of parameters in a Cauchy distribution with specific variations and how sample size affects this bias, demonstrating that while bias generally decreases as sample size increases, it can still be significant even with large sample sizes.

A new statistical method is developed for assessing sample sizes in basket trials that analyze multiple subpopulations separately. Our approach allows information sharing between these populations, like a hybrid of targeted and basket trials. We present formulas for estimating required trial sizes for each subpopulation and demonstrate these through two real-world examples. Bayesian theory justifies our methodology, specifically using the reference prior distribution to formulate the predictive distribution of unknown parameters given limited initial data. This Bayesian predictive distribution serves as the basis for our proposed methodology. We also compare this method with alternative designs, such as targeted trials with fixed parameters and basket trials analyzing combined data, using metrics like treatment effect estimation accuracy and predicted trial sizes. The benefits of our approach are particularly evident in scenarios with limited treatment effects and limited availability of data.

A novel strategy, referred to as LPV sequential loop tightening (LSLT), has been developed to address the challenges of designing high-performance motion systems that can be easily manufactured and operate under a variety of conditions. This approach builds on the concept of sequential loop tightening (SLT) but incorporates the effects of parameter variability. A detailed investigation of SLS and LSLT is conducted using a precise motion system as a case study, involving an LPV model derived from a motion system with a servo drive. Motion commands are generated using model predictive control (MPC) based on the LPV model, with the parameters adjusted in real-time to maintain optimal performance. Key findings emerge from the comparison of SLS and LSLT, indicating that SLS leads to significant limitations on motion performance and suggests an alternative method for determining the optimal sampling period. Furthermore, LSLT is shown to be applicable in real-time and can be implemented using an off-the-shelf controller, such as the PI controller, to achieve high-precision motion.

We introduce a novel deep learning approach, partial registration network (PRNet), specifically designed for aligning partial point cloud models. Building on supervised learning principles, PRNet leverages paired point cloud datasets to develop a model that enables registration in a self-supervised manner. The algorithm enables the alignment of partial models against a target shape through iterative optimization, producing a loss function that facilitates convergence. Empirical evaluation of PRNet on diverse datasets reveals its ability to achieve registration accuracy on complex models, with results exceeding current methods.

A group G exhibits property $R_\infty$ if all automorphisms of countably infinite, discrete, non-locally-finite rooted graphs result in a truncated double action that is freely finitely-rationalizable. We establish that groups of the form $\mathbb{Z}[\frac{1}{2}]\ltimes A$ where $A$ is either $\mathbb{Z}$ or $\mathbb{Z}[\frac{1}{2}]$, demonstrates the $R_\infty$ property. $\mathbb{Z}[\frac{1}{2}]\ltimes \mathbb{Z}$ specifically does not fulfill the $R_\infty$ characteristic for the group $\Gamma(2)$.

We assess the potential of future high-energy colliders to detect instability in the Standard Model, specifically the Higgs boson, at three experimental stages: beyond the current LHC, at a upgraded LHC with higher luminosity, and at future new colliders with higher energy but slower production, such as the CLIC or ILC. The likelihood of discovering new physics beyond the Standard Model at each stage is evaluated based on theoretical assumptions and actual achievements in similar studies from the past. Assuming the Standard Model instability confirms to be around 1 MeV, the following findings emerge: an upgraded but higher-luminosity LHC has a slim prospect of detecting the instability; future colliders with higher energy but slower production have a slightly better but still limited potential; and, sensitivity in electroweak states, such as the Higgs boson and W boson, could be improved with optimized searches not relying on theoretical assumptions.

A new technique is developed to process time-sensitive data from ultra-fast experiments using an approach based on optimization in a trajectory basis. This technique is successfully tested on data from experiments involving X-ray scattering and electron diffraction to analyze the breakdown of molecules. Results from applying the technique accurately match experimental findings and highlight key molecular dynamics, furthermore providing reliable error estimates. Technique variations are suggested for handling specific experimental challenges.

The study focuses on the mass spectra of $D^*$, and $D^*_s$ mesons using the QCD sum rule, and QCD perturbation theory. The calculated mass values are then compared with actual data. Furthermore, the study distributes decay width information according to different quark interaction channels for $D^* \to D + \gamma$, $D^*_s \to D_s \gamma$, and $\kappa_{D^*} \kappa_{\gamma} $, and $\kappa_{D^*_s} \kappa_{\gamma}$, and finds the results are in acceptable agreement with current data. The study also finds the results are in acceptable agreement with current data. The distribution profiles of $D^*$ and $D^*_s$ mesons are generated using Bethe-Salpeter wave functions and the result shows that the relative probability of $D^*$ appearing as $D^* \to D + \gamma$ or $D^* \to \rho \gamma$ process is 0.356, and for $D^*_s$ as $D^*_s \to D_s \gamma$ or $D^*_s \to \phi \gamma$ process is 0.314.

We investigate key properties of several types of Gelfand-Shilov spaces, which are characterized by the decay of their smooth functions and their Fourier transforms. The nontriviality of these spaces, specifically ${\Sigma}^{\sigma}_s$, is shown to depend on the values of $s$ and ${\sigma}$ being greater than 1. The text further presents growth estimates for functions within one-parameter spaces, and it also establishes relationships between short-time Fourier transforms and these spaces. Moreover, conditions are established to ensure that Toeplitz operators are continuous when applied to functions within one-parameter spaces.

Automatically identifying organs and tissues in medical imaging is essential for both medical imaging analysis and clinical applications, particularly for procedures that currently rely on time-consuming manual segmentation.  Recent advances in deep learning have led to the development of unsupervised domain adaptation techniques for mapping low-dose imaging data to diagnostic doses, drawing on a wealth of unlabelled diagnostic scans.  However, these methods typically require a comprehensive set of reference organs tagged in low-dose images to perform adaptation.  This study addresses the more general challenge of marking organs in unlabelled diagnostic scans to support a range of diagnostic tasks.  To achieve this, it employs a CycleGAN and division all the way GAN to convert unlabeled images into diagnostic scans with annotated organs.  This virtual marking is then combined with domain adaptation techniques to map low-dose images to diagnostic scans with the same virtual organ markers.  Experiments with abdominal and head scans demonstrate the effectiveness of the method in producing accurate organ segmentations.

Research has concentrated on generating plausible future motions using various future prediction methods.  In this study, a novel RNN architecture called RNN with Feature mapping is proposed, incorporating an RBF kernel into the feature mapping function to predict likely future actions from given state sequences.  The proposed F-RNN can capture both short-term and long-term movements by leveraging two distinct feature mapping functions - one for the initial state and another for future time steps.  The framework's ability to adapt to different input data is achieved through the parameterization of the F-RNN's parameters, along with using an additional loss function to maintain consistency between predicted and actual future motion.  The proposed F-RNN with GRU and LSTU cells outperformed existing methods on benchmark datasets for human action prediction like HMDB-51, UCF101, and UT-Interaction.

Our investigation into a remarkable stellar flare seen from AD Leo in 1985 offers novel insights, combining a realistic model of the near-ultraviolet spectral range with precise observations from the IUE. Employing the most current understanding of line blends and photospheric spectrum characteristics from far-ultraviolet data, our analysis reconciles two sets of observations, thereby enhancing the understanding of line formation processes in early ultraviolet spectra. Our findings indicate that the rapid shift of low ionization lines seen in IUE observations towards longer wavelengths can be fully attributed to the sudden cooling of the post-flare plasma, rather than the direct impact of line formation. Additionally, our simulation reveals that the significant shift of the 3130 Å line towards longer wavelengths can be primarily attributed to the rapid expansion of plasma at 10,000 K or warmer. Our study also identifies unknown line blends in IUE spectra around 2830 Å and 3130 Å, and predicts that a short-wavelength part of the near-ultraviolet range may contain previously unrecognized emission lines of low ionization. Our simulation of the AD Leo flare also illustrates the rapid formation and decay of high-altitude structures in early stages of the flare, as well as the rapid expansion of lower atmospheric features taking around 2 minutes to reach visibility.

We have completed a study on the deformation of G2 instantons within nearly G2 manifolds. Our method involves converting the G2 instanton equation into a zero curvature condition for a specific connection on a associated bundle. By establishing the isomorphism between this connection and a subconnection of a larger one, constructed from a nearly G2 manifold, we found that the spectrum of the twisted Dirac operator on the six-manifold is integral and upper bounded. Additionally, we characterized the deformation of G2 instantons and calculated the deformation of the associated twisted connection.

A bounded linear operator $T$ on a complex Hilbert space with a countable basis is referred to as C-normal if it satisfies a particular condition under the action of a conjugation operation. Specifically, $T$ can be said to be C-normal if there exists a conjugation operation $C$ on $H$ such that $TC^\ast CT = C^\ast T^\ast T$. In the context of function mappings, a self-map $\varphi$ of the open unit disc can be described using a linear fractional expression. This work investigates the conditions under which the composition operator $C_\varphi$ and weighted composition operator $W_{\psi, \varphi}$, where $\psi$ is another function, are both C-normal operators for specific conjugation operations $C$ and $\psi$.

This paper delves into a type of sequence that adheres to specific criteria related to partitions and avoids certain patterns. By linking these sequences to a graph-based game, where players take steps on a graph based on a numerical system, we've been able to find relationships between these sequences and the way players move on the graph. This connection allows us to count how many different ways there are to move on the graph, which also answers a previous mathematical question. Moreover, our work is connected to a broader set of mathematical ideas called irreducible characters.

Recent cutting-edge conditional GAN models for point cloud modeling have achieved remarkable results, but they still struggle with stability and efficient training. To address these issues, a novel deep learning approach called TPC is introduced, which develops a reliable and efficient method for stabilizing the training of conditional GANs on point cloud datasets. TPC achieves this by incorporating an advanced transformation-based smoothing technique into its model architecture. This approach first applies a suite of primitive transformations to latent code inputs in a CNN-based generator network. By standardizing the range of these basic transformations, the stability of model training is significantly enhanced. Experimental evaluations of TPC on three diverse point cloud datasets demonstrate its performance superiority over existing methods. Notably, TPC sets a new benchmark in Fr\'echet Inception Distance (FID) score of 15.53 on Church dataset, surpassing the previous best score of 19.18. Additionally, TPC shows impressive efficiency with a reduced number of parameters compared to its competitors.

The rapid advancement of Frequency Modulated Continuous Wave (FMCW) radar technology is transforming various industries, including automotive and industrial sectors, with its ability to provide precise distance and velocity measurements for surrounding objects. As a result, integrating FMCW radar units into existing systems to ensure safety and reliability has become a pressing concern. To address potential interference between these devices, researchers have investigated and proposed methods to mitigate the effects of such interference. This study builds upon previous research by examining two medium access control techniques, slotted ALOHA and CSMA, in the context of FMCW radar networks and exploring alternative solutions to address the complex issues surrounding radar technology utilization.

We explore a unique setup where two photons from a two-photon absorption process, facilitated by a entwined system, interact in an Hong-Ou-Mandel interferometer. The entwined system's properties are chosen such that their interaction with photons resonates with a specific energy level. The entwined system can be realized as a two-qubit system with correlated initial states and radiative coupling to an external electromagnetic field representing the optical field. The setup includes a beam splitter and two output paths where detection occurs. The outcomes of what would normally be HOM interference experiments from this setup are a reduced correlation between the entwined system's state and photon presence at the two outputs, as seen through a analysis in a Fock basis and partial logarithmic concavity. The effect scales with the hypergeometric function and depends on the two photon absorption rate, and results in a reduced maximum correlation that scales with the entwined system's coupling strength to the external field. The absence of a conditional change in the entwined system's state when one photon is present leads to a lack of complete anti-correlation between system and photon, as seen through examination of various spectral properties using a spectral decomposition and Fock space expansion. The outcome can be quantified through examination of a partial transferability of spectral weight from the entwined system to the photons. We establish that circle action equivariant elliptic cohomology of complex projective spaces derived from finite dimensional graded vector spaces V has a logarithmic expression, which generalizes the result for complex projective spaces of specific dimensions.

Temporal knowledge graph inference involves reconstructing incomplete graphs with missing entities and relationships. Building upon past achievements, we address the challenge by proposing a universal approach for knowledge graph inference. The method employs a low-rank matrix factorization technique that enables the representation of entities using a continuous, linear structure. We develop a two-phase inference process for ranking potential relationships and relationships with a given entity. The method refrains from using temporal information, relying instead on a model that integrates with any temporal knowledge graph model to produce consistent representations. In experiments, our approach surpasses current state-of-the-art methods in MTL-KGI for MWP, MWP, and MWP+ metrics, with notable improvements over fast knowledge graph inference methods.

In the field of sound simulation, the method has been developed to recreate the intense sound produced by objects hitting the ground. Unfortunately, the technique has yet to be widely adopted due to its excessive computational cost. We have now developed an efficient approach for a common sound effect by creating a simple algorithm that accounts for the basic factors contributing to ground sound. As a result, the method can be easily integrated into existing simulation techniques without significantly increasing computational requirements.

A conventional view holds that achieving Bell nonlocality necessitates a violation of a Bell inequality, yet this paper presents an alternative perspective. Our model, comprised of two qubits, demonstrates the impossibility of forming a pure, entangled state when two particles are in a two-body pure state not spanning a one-dimensional space. This model illustrates that non-locality without inequality can be exemplified through complete lack of correlation between measurements of distinct qubits, as well as the inability to form a narrow, one-dimensional state from their combined measurements, even when individual measurements are purely probabilistic. As such, non-locality without inequality is shown to stem from non-optimal correlations rather than necessarily violating a Bell inequality. This understanding could potentially shift the current understanding of achieving Bell nonlocality and for this reason the example presented remains anonymous for the time being.

Building on previous work by Deshpande et al. introduces the concept of flat lines, a graphical representation of loop equivariant elliptic invariants, which enlightens the relationship between the Bishof-Müller map and the Tanisaki map. Furthermore, the paper explores new applications of the Bishof-Müller map in the contexts of loop equivariant elliptic cohomology and Maxime Ulmer's research on half-bundles.

A newly created hydrogen boride compound, diboride MH4B2 ($Pnnm$ structure), has been studied using first principles calculations. Our analysis, based on density functional theory, shows that MH4B2 has electrical properties that can be described as metallic, with a small energy gap at the Fermi level. Our study, however, disagrees with a recent claim that MH4B2 exhibits superconductivity. To understand the mechanism behind the previously reported superconductivity, we investigated various factors that could contribute to it. Our results, however, reveal that the previously reported superconducting behavior is likely due to artificial cell replication and an incorrect chemical potential, as well as strong chemical bonds between hydrogen and boron atoms. Our study also shows that a high pressure of 50 GPa has a limited impact on MH4B2's superconductivity. But when we used a more realistic model that accounts for electron-phonon interactions, our results reveal that MH4B2 does not exhibit superconductivity, with a negligible effect of pressure on its electronic structure.

This study explores the application of fractional programming in managing the
operation of multiple systems simultaneously, addressing the run allocation
problem over shared storage partitions. A proposed solution involves modeling
this problem as a fractional linear program which can be solved through
transforming it into a finite number of linear programs by applying specific
technological advancements. The method employs partition and scan techniques to
break down the problem, yielding an efficient solution that can be implemented
using standard mathematical programming software directly, thereby bypassing the
need for complex special orderings or solutions tailored to specific problem
characteristics.

We introduce the concept of charmability for countable groups, which involves a recursive sequence of finite subgroup inclusions that prioritize larger subgroups. This idea parallels the notion of minimality in topological dynamics. By developing this concept, we're able to prove that any countable group exhibiting charm can be topologically realized as a group of transformations with a topological basis consisting of automorphisms of a tree that have finite stabilization. Additionally, we establish that a group possesses this characteristic if and only if it has no proper, finite-by-abelian quotients. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this new concept redefines the classification of group stiffness, effectively extending it to all countable groups while retaining its topological implications. Specifically, a group is said to be stiffally minimal if and only if it exhibits charmability. Using this framework, we're also able to derive a corrected version of Ghys' conjecture regarding group stiffness, particularly for groups of prime-order.

Automated driving systems designed to operate in case of failure demand robust architecture and contingency planning mechanisms. To ensure high-level system reliability, even in the event of multiple component failures, an advanced backup system is essential. This article showcases a logical framework that validates and assesses a safety-critical system's ability to operate reliably during component failures. The proposed framework consists of three layers: 

1. Monitoring of system performance and health. 
2. Identification of critical failures requiring backup systems or manual intervention. 
3. Activation of fallback protocols to maintain system functionality.

The presented strategy is applied to a practical driving assistant system and formally verified using a model checker, thereby ensuring its adherence to this framework.

We propose a novel methodical approach for clustering dynamic systems based on their behavior over extended periods, using data-driven methods. Our approach initially utilizes an already established data-driven model to minimize a cost function, which measures the differences between clusters using an objective function that weighs trajectory similarities and durations. We then develop an optimization problem to determine cluster boundaries, which are represented by decision variables that adhere to certain constraints, ultimately leading to a solution that optimizes system partitioning. Our approach is applied to two case studies, with positive results. Specifically, it successfully clusters an example single-rocket dynamic system with five distinct states of activity and a collection of 11 lunar landing scenarios modeled using a 10th-order nonlinear differential algebraic equation system, which accurately characterized various phases of these missions.

Our detailed examination of historical methods in Leibnizian calculus reveals that each corresponds to one of three distinct frameworks for handling infinite quantities, which we have systematically organized and explained for the benefit of modern mathematicians and scientists. The first framework involves the use of infinitesimals as primary entities, governing a formalized logic system as proposed by Robinson in the mid-20th century. The second framework incorporates an specialized version of Dedekind cuts, integrated within the axiomatic structure of real numbers as per Cantor's definition. Finally, the third framework relies on a iterative process of partitioning, aligning with the Epimorphism framework for constructing the real numbers as a representation of the continuum.

Large-scale cosmological studies are becoming increasingly feasible due to the accessibility of HI data through intensity mapping techniques, which can be implemented using telescopes such as the Square Kilometre Array. Although theoretical predictions for cosmological signals exist, the impact of foreground removal methods remains poorly understood in terms of their effects on these signals. Here, a framework for analyzing disturbances is applied to study the spatial patterns of temperature and redshift in HI intensity mapping data, with predictions based on realistic observations. Additionally, the implementation of a linear foreground removal method is evaluated in terms of its effects on the estimated power spectrum of cosmological fluctuations.

We examine the connections between three key properties of Hilbert space operators: independence, infinite extent, and boundedness. Specifically, we've established the following relationships: (1) For a compact operator T on an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space H, having no finite-dimensional invariant subspaces implies it has a non-trivial Volterra part, connected to but distinct from those of quasi-nilpotent compact operators with no finite-dimensional invariant subspaces. (2) For any operator on a infinite-dimensional space, having no finite-dimensional invariant subspaces means it has a non-trivial Volterra part. (3) For a bounded operator on an infinite-dimensional space, having no finite-dimensional invariant subspaces is equivalent to having a non-trivial Volterra part.

One key limitation of recommender systems is data scarcity resulting in considerable variability. Various approaches have been implemented to optimize the bias-variance equilibrium utilizing supplementary information. In particular, methods incorporating text-based document modeling have significantly improved accuracy by incorporating data like reviews, summaries, and narratives when user-item rating matrices are sparse. Nonetheless, these models are inadequate to learn user and item features. Collaborative filtering methods, including user-based and item-based, due to their efficiency and clarity, have long been utilized in recommender systems by generating profiles for each user and item based on their historically interacted items and users. Although these methods are simple, they are susceptible to over-fitting and data scarcity. Our proposed method, called DeepCD, integrates the strengths of deep learning-based document models and traditional collaborative filtering methods by combining their representations into a unified model. We also present an unsupervised word embedding technique, where words from reviews and narratives are embedded into a common space alongside existing words. Our empirical results demonstrate that DeepCD surpasses comparative methods with improved accuracy and higher coverage when evaluated on two real-world datasets.

We examine the openness of the generalized Lindeberg condition for matrix-valued variables and establish a conditional central limit theorem under a specific type of openness, B-type, which is associated with the asymptotic covariance of partially permuted matrix elements. Additionally, we investigate the B-type openness of certain matrix-based averages, such as those originating from non-commutative statistical mechanics, and demonstrate the fulfillment of a particular type of type B openness known as strong type B openness, which is linked to the Wigner matrix and certain other spectral ensembles.

The initial deployment of autonomous robots starts with robots executing the same program simultaneously. This work reevaluates timer-based properties for facilitating coordinated robot behavior in finite timed environments. Leveraging a graph-theoretic model, we investigate the model-checking problem for detecting inconsistencies in robot programs. Although timer constraints are solvable in timer-related models, the underlying transformation presents explication issues. We address this limitation by developing a more appropriate model-checking framework, which integrates automata and graph models, thereby allowing us to provide efficient algorithms with improved complexity.

The decay reactions $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi f_0(980)$ and $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi
a_0(980)$ are examined in detail. Attention is focused on the production of the
$f_0(980)$ and $a_0(980)$ resonances through the $s\bar s$ component of the antiparticle
and its subsequent interaction with $J/\psi$. The study takes into account the
possibility of rescattering effects influencing the final observation of the $f_0(980)
a_0(980)$ blend. The branching ratios for both decay reactions are calculated in
three different scenarios: (i) purely resonant contributions, (ii) dominant
resonant contributions accompanied by secondary effects and (iii) predominant
resonant contributions accompanied by a nonresonant background. In the first case,
the branching ratios range between $1.52 \times 10^{-6}$ and $2.28 $\times 10^{-6}$
brances. In the second case, they vary between $1.82 \times 10^{-6}$ and $2.53 $\times
10^{-6}$ branches. In the third case, they range between $1.52 \times 10^{-6}$ and
$2.82 $\times 10^{-6}$ branches. Additionally, our study derives upper limits
