This research focuses on finding a key characteristic of set-valued mappings, known as the core, and establishing existence criteria for these mappings under strict stability conditions. Furthermore, we present concise algorithmic solutions that demonstrate the Lipschitz property in various scenarios, including single-point mappings, mappings with finite codomain, and those with codomain $R^n$. These results are applied to analyze certain nonlinear equations involving set-valued mappings and their corresponding implicit versions.

The objectives of this research are to (1) demonstrate that the likelihood model can serve as a reliable framework for examining comparative non-transitivity, (2) develop a method to identify the specific aspects of a likelihood that give rise to cyclic preferences, and (3) present testable predictions based on this likelihood. A particular type of model, known as the multivariate probit model, is utilized for the purposes of illustration. The model is applied to data from a well-known experiment involving preference cycles and the results show significant evidence of significant rank correlations among the parameters, indicating the existence of non-trivial structural characteristics. The likelihood model is found to effectively capture the cyclic structure of these preferences without relying on complex auxiliary models.

Across various software systems, run-time set-ups are fundamental in launching applications, yet they can be cumbersome and cumbersome, particularly when numerous preparations are needed. Although compile-time tools can streamline this process by reducing the time required for set-ups, they often fail to recognize the inherent possibilities for simplifying the set-up process until run-time has already occurred. As a result, these tools are generally unable to make such optimizations. This paper addresses this issue by investigating the potential for reducing the complexity of set-ups during compile-time and demonstrating the results of an empirical study involving 12 benchmarks from different fields with a high number of set-ups. By analyzing the code of these benchmarks and employing a profile-guided approach, we were able to reduce the complexity of set-ups by an average of 66.15% in 10 out of the 12 benchmarks, which in turn led to a significant decrease of 95.25% in the total time required for set-ups in five of these benchmarks.

Light dark matter particles, weighing less than a GeV, offer an attractive solution over established models. Directly detecting such particles, however, poses significant challenges, particularly when the recoil energy required to detect them is low. A novel detection method based on electron ionization following nuclear recoil has been proposed, providing hope for detecting sub-GeV dark matter particles that may elude other detection methods. Despite using above-ground, thin-window detectors with previously established methods, our simulations indicate that this new method can achieve a significant improvement, reaching a detection sensitivity thirty times greater for 10-megaelectronvolt dark matter particles. Furthermore, our algorithm is capable of distinguishing the light dark matter signal from background noise with high accuracy.

This study explores the dynamics of a two-level system (atom) interacting with a single-mode quantized electromagnetic field, under the condition of initial entanglement between the atom and the field. Contrary to the standard Jaynes-Cummings model, our model operates differently, yet simultaneously, due to the field's initial state preparation. Notably, our findings reveal the occurrence of rapid Rabi oscillations, reduced entanglement, and an increased transmission rate of the electromagnetic field. The rate of entanglement decay and field transmission can be manipulated through the adjustment of initial field parameters. Additionally, the system's behavior exhibits duality, which is confirmed by plotting the phase diagrams of entanglement and transmission.

Measuring the inter-beat interval from an ECG signal is a critical task in cardiac health monitoring. Researchers have explored deep learning techniques for this purpose, focusing on R-peak detection to estimate IBIs. Most studies utilize data augmentation to enhance model performance. Our innovative approach introduces the Tiramisu network, an iterative deep learning model that integrates R-peak detection and IBI estimation without the need for augmented data. By optimizing each stage of the model, we have achieved an average error rate of 9.43 milliseconds, surpassing existing methods.

We use Onsager variational methods to find solutions for models that deviate from the original Ornstein-Uhlenbeck theory, specifically active Brownian particles with non-linear forces and noise with non-zero correlation times. By generalizing the Wiger-Hirschfelder equation, we find a new set of equations governing the probability distribution in the active Brownian particle model with non-linear forces, noise with an arbitrary decay rate, and noise with non-zero correlation times. Additionally, we confirm that applying harmonic and bistable potentials to the Wiger-Hirschfelder equation recovers known results for these specific cases.

The capture of human movement has been focused on by many researchers, with an eye to utilizing pose data in real-world applications.  A recent trend has seen the utilization of single cameras to capture multiview data, with resulting images being combined into a full scene representation.  However, working with actual three-dimensional human movement for genuine applications necessitates the capture of pose data from multiple, varied viewpoints.  In this research, a novel dataset called HUMBI was created, with the goal of tackling key difficulties in the capture and tracking of human movement.  This dataset includes detailed movements captured from 8 different viewpoints, with the resulting images processed through a cutting-edge 3D pose estimation technique.  The resulting tracked data includes a range of difficult-to-capture movements, totaling 544,000 poses, with a particularly complex sequence of 3000 poses also included.  A benchmark challenge has also been established, with the goal of evaluating and refining the current state of art in human movement capture and tracking.

Several neural models have achieved significant cross-lingual transfer results by leveraging information from related languages, but their effectiveness depends heavily on the specific task and resources available, which can be scarce for lesser-studied languages. Our proposed approach utilizes a task representation learned from one language to provide weak guidance for training a model to perform the same task in another language, without requiring extensive language-specific training. It enables model-agnostic transfer by leveraging pre-optimized task representations, which can be applied to various models through cross-lingual alignment. Experiment results show that our method achieves notable performance gains on NLP benchmarks such as sentiment analysis and question-answering in multiple languages, including those with limited data and no cross-lingual word embeddings.

A prominent video super-resolution method, Video Super-Resolution with Fully Self-Extracted Features, has a limitation in handling torn and distorted temporal predictions due to a lack of direct supervision. To address this issue, BasicVSR++, an advanced version of the method, utilizes multi-scale temporal propagation for intact area estimation and precise alignment of distorted frames. Leveraging the strengths of deep video propagation and neighboring frame interpolation, BasicVSR++ efficiently generates comprehensive and sharp predictions. Notably, the approach outperforms existing video super-resolution methods in terms of PSNR and SSIM performance in various scales and has a relatively lightweight footprint, making it a practical solution for real-world applications.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning settings. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that using
a single learned dynamics model for multiple tasks may actually decrease the
performance and lead to task confusion. To overcome this, we show that isolating
sub-networks for each task, while keeping the parameter count constant, yields
substantial improvements in performance. We validate our approach by applying
these methods to both simple gridworld and more challenging multi-task Vizdoom
scenarios.

We have developed a novel method to create a comprehensive catalogue of optimal heat engines operating within specific timesframes, powered by two-level systems interacting with heat baths. The method involves manipulating the initial and final states of the system to achieve maximum work output, subject to certain control restrictions. By applying a semi-infinite programming technique, we were able to obtain precise numerical results for a range of operating conditions. The findings demonstrate that there is an intricate balance between the time frame, work output, and internal energy changes, and that partial control limitations significantly affect optimal performance. Moreover, the method can be expanded to tackle more complex problems involving multi-heat-source engines.

This research proposes a probabilistic model for analyzing the impact of combined hurricane and storm surge events on large power grids. To simulate real-world hurricane scenarios, the study generates storm paths based on historical data, and corresponding wind and storm surge probabilities are established through statistical analysis. A Monte-Carlo approach is used to evaluate system reliability, and our findings are validated by applying this model to the 2008 hurricane season in the US Gulf Coast.

This article formulates the Three Balls Theorem for functions governed by the Dirac operator in a specifically structured complex space. This is accomplished by first establishing a structured representation for these functions within a triple ball configuration. Building on this, we prove that a weighted sum of the first few derivative components of these functions remains positive within this structure, exceeding the weighted sum of the corresponding derivative components in an adjacent triple ball configuration by a certain margin. This margin is shown to be influenced by a relevant scaling parameter and the self-respective properties of these functions, here termed positivity retention parameter. This result extends known findings related to harmonic functions and the rotational symmetry in Clifford analysis.

We examine two iterated map systems that demonstrate analogous behavior on the boundary between stochastic and deterministic dynamics. The first system consists of a pair of Baker maps, applied independently on two intervals, which generate a set of invariant measures maximizing entropy within a two-dimensional space. This work redevelops the numerical techniques used to analyze a related system in a previous study. The second system involves a coupling of the Dyck system with a chaotic component, which switches between two different mapping functions based on whether a system's orbit is within a given interval or not. This latter system, identical to one explored by Rehberger in 2005 in terms of its map coupling, exhibits a phase transition at its critical boundary, marking the transition from stochastic to deterministic behavior. In contrast to expectations based on the idea that entropy accessibility is invariant in such systems, the new results show that this property is not maintained. The present study identifies the origin of this effect as a consequence of a sudden shift in how measures are distributed on certain fractal sets within these systems, which occurs at the critical boundary for the second system and is a latent feature in the first system as well.

Following the groundbreaking detection of the scalar boson with a 125 GeV mass, known as the Higgs particle, numerous theories have suggested the presence of additional, heavier scalars. These predictions are integral to the Standard Model of particle physics and are also prevalent in many alternative theoretical frameworks beyond the Standard Model. Research has highlighted the significance of searching for these scalars through the process of pair production at future high-energy particle accelerators, specifically proton-proton colliders with 27 and 31 TeV center-of-mass energy, and future electron-positron colliders operating at the Z-boson mass and beyond. This review focuses on the detection and identification of an expanded scalar sector at these upcoming collider platforms.

This study introduces quasi-periodic WaveNet, an advanced generative model based on the original WaveNet architecture. To create more effective conditional probabilistic models, waveNet was enhanced with a pitch-dependent expanded convolution neural network. The novel addition helps to control the pitch, allowing for more accurate low-frequency protection in voice synthesis. The modified network achieves a significant reduction in computational requirements without compromising its high-fidelity audio output, achieving results comparable to the state-of-the-art performance.

To tackle the inherent shortcomings of recommendation systems, including user preference diversity, data sparsity, and subjective interpretation, we introduce a novel approach based on biclustering. The proposed method utilizes Cluster-based Latent Factor (CLF) models, which incorporate bicluster weights and user-bicluster vectors to address the complexity of collaborative filtering algorithms. By leveraging preference patterns in rating matrices, CLF algorithms develop strategies to handle cases where there might be no optimal biclusters statistically. The algorithm generates and refines biclusters through two stages, followed by an optimization process using alternating least squares (ALQS), outperforming state-of-the-art recommenders according to comprehensive experiments on six real-world datasets.

Significant progress has been made in studying the solar magnetic cycle, thanks to high-resolution solar spectra obtained by the HARPS-N instrument. By using state-of-the-art sunspots and faculae models, researchers have developed several new indicators of solar magnetic activity that can complement existing indicators, such as the Facular Brightness Temperature Anomaly ($\Delta T_F$) and the Net Facular Brightness Temperature Anomaly ($\Delta T_{net}$). These new indicators, along with $\Delta T_F$ and $\Delta T_{net}$, are being evaluated based on their correlation with solar cycle 24's characteristics and other cycles on file. Furthermore, we've explored the prospects of using specific magnetic activity features, such as the strong far ultraviolet (FUV) lines of C II, O III, and He I, to improve the understanding of solar faculae and bright granulation. The observation of these features in future solar spectra could provide more accurate indicators of solar magnetic activity.

To differentiate between zero-bias peaks originating from Majorana and other sources, we introduce a novel technique. When a resistive electrode is introduced in contact with a Majorana island, Ohmic dissipation in the presence of a bias voltage leads to a substantial decrease in the zero-bias peak height associated with Majorana modes. In contrast, for non-Majorana zero-bias peaks, we demonstrate that the contribution of the resistive electrode's quantum resistance can result in an increased peak height. The utility of our proposed method is further demonstrated through an exploration of its performance under conditions of approximate, not exact dissipation.

Mark Kisin initially proposed the concept of B-categorical marks as a localized version of the Mark Kisin's B-marks introduced in his 2007 paper 'Twisted self-products and endomorphisms'. In 2021, Matthew Ghoul and Michael Schein further developed this concept, exploring B-categorical marks in relation to twisted self products. Building upon these prior works, we present an alternative approach to B-categorical marks, specifically for the case of Shimura varieties of finite type. Within this context, we demonstrate that B-categorical marks can be expressed as the B-marks multiplied by the zeroth Galois cohomology class of an appropriate sheaf, depending on the case at hand. In addition, we establish several key findings. Firstly, B-categorical marks are 1-marks. Secondly, B-categorical marks are B-marks if and only if they are B-marks of twisted self products. Thirdly, B-categorical marks do not necessarily correspond to B-marks of the twisted varieties themselves. Lastly, we illustrate our findings through examples.

Effective use of style transfer techniques depends on a clear definition of style, allowing for consistent and reproducible results. This clarity is particularly important in color-critical fields, where color consistency is paramount for accuracy. We develop a novel approach, combining a forward and inverse color mapping algorithm, to accurately transfer colors from reference images to input images. The forward algorithm applies a neural network to predict reference colors, while the inverse algorithm reconstructs these colors from the modified images using a convolutional network. The presence of noise in the input images necessitates a cleanup process, to remove non-stationary noise and stabilize the color mapping. We employ a stylized image pair denoising model, inspired by structure and texture extraction methods, to eliminate noise from the modified images. The algorithm's effectiveness has been proven through a set of comprehensive tests including, color restoration, image colorization, multi-spectral to multi-band image conversion and map colorization. The results demonstrate our method outperforms comparative approaches in various color-critical applications.

This technical report showcases the winning model developed for the AQTC task at the LOVEU contest, whose results were announced at CVPR 2022. The proposed model integrates top-performing methods from recent research to address the complex multi-choice, multi-stop, and multi-agent nature of the AQTC task. Specifically, it combines a robust agent routing algorithm with a predictive model that leverages contextual information and temporal dependencies. Extensive experimental evaluations demonstrate the exceptional performance of the proposed model, whose outstanding results validate the significance of the techniques employed.

As snow falls into the ground's atmosphere, it undergoes a complex process that is not yet fully understood. Selective sweeping, a theory proposing that larger snowflakes have an advantage in the process due to their size, has been long-standing, but there has been limited scientific evidence to support it. Through high-resolution simulations of snowflake interactions with atmospheric turbulence, we discovered that smaller flakes are less likely to survive collisions, effectively giving larger flakes an opportunity to reach the ground first. Our research provides significant evidence for the selective sweeping theory and its potential implications for snowflake evolution are also explored.

robots navigating through unfamiliar environments face uncertainty in their path predictions due to incomplete map data and varying terrain characteristics, which can lead to misjudging the feasibility of their planned routes and wasting time on unessential computations. Our approach addresses this issue by incorporating a novel data acquisition system that utilizes the robot's sensor data, including information from global navigation satellites, inertial sensors, and other sources, to decide when and where to collect more information before starting their journey. When activated, this acquisition system takes the robot's current measurements and estimated map data as inputs, weighing the utility of new data against the costs of and constraints on the robot's path, which ultimately influences the map update decision. Once a decision is made, the updated map data are used to reassess the robot's path, leading to a new set of actions that are repeated until a predetermined stopping criterion is met. Our proposed system is driven by a reinforcement learning framework that balances map completion and exploration-loss, and it is applied to a number of scenarios in an autonomous robot simulation environment.

In the field of particle physics, researchers need to process vast amounts of data produced by detectors, with the current Big Data paradigm facing challenges in dealing with sparse, irregular data from 3D detectors. To tackle this issue, a novel data reduction framework is introduced, utilizing a bicephalous convolutional autoencoder that can both learn and apply sparse data transformations to reduce data redundancy. By leveraging this framework with a shared hidden representation, an autoencoder is enabled to capture common patterns in input data, and subsequently, redundant information can be efficiently eliminated from experimental data. Through applications to simulated data from the Time Projection Chamber at the IHEP Beijing, it was found that the proposed framework results in a significant reduction of data redundancy across all three spatial directions, with minimal loss of signal information, thereby validating its effectiveness for use in future particle physics research experiments.

In a Finzi gauge gravity theory, galaxy clusters are analyzed using King profiles, with their properties (concentration, mass radius, total mass) affected by a crucial parameter from the theory. A numerical routine is developed to solve Einstein's modified equations, allowing for the calculation of King models with variable polytropic indices. While the standard polytropic index is $2$, it varies with distance in Finzi gravity models, resulting in divergent masses for these galaxy clusters. This study computes mass integration for various polytropic indices, with the result that only up to a specific index can these clusters remain bound; indices higher than this result in negative or vanishing masses. We investigate how these changes in the polytropic index impact the 3D mass profiles, mass radii, central densities, and concentration indices of galaxy clusters. Furthermore, we examine the relationship between mass radii and other core properties in galaxy clusters, including their dependence on concentration, with the goal of validating the predictions of Finzi gravity models and their consistency with diverse galaxy cluster observations.

A type of geometric hypergraph called cGH(n,d) consists of a collection of subsets containing at most d points each, characterized by being convex in a d-dimensional space. Research has demonstrated that for a geometric hypergraph meeting these criteria, its H-rebarr(d) value will be roughly n^(1/(2+ε)) if d is three or greater. Here, H-rebarr(d) represents the maximum number for a geometric hypergraph under such constraints that can be formed using a value 'r' for a specific k, resulting in points arranged in a geometric fashion. Investigating this area of study, we identify cGH(n,4) instances where the H-rebarr(4) value reaches n^(1/3). This research also explores the challenges associated with proving a theoretical upper limit for geometric hypergraphs, even with simplified convex geometries.

To study direct neutron resonance capture and other alternative proton capture processes, the $^6$Li+$^51$V system was investigated. Using a merged-beams technique, experimental cross-sections for $^6$Li + $^51$V elastic scattering and breakup were obtained. These data, combined with theoretical calculations based on the finite range distorted wave Born approximation, led to the derivation of inclusive $\alpha$ cross-sections. The calculated inclusive $\alpha$ cross-sections matched the experimental results, and the obtained angular distributions and energy spectra showed characteristics typical of compound nuclear effects, indicating that high-lying states of the compound nucleus $^57$Ta were involved. Additionally, the analysis of the angular distributions and energy spectra of the fragments suggested the existence of two distinct nuclear states at excitation energies above the $^{57}$Ta ground state.

A study was conducted on the climbing behavior of Pacific lampreys, specifically how they use a unique process called'mucus-assisted adhesion' (MAA) to ascend from the bottom of a tank to a horizontal surface covered with a non-stick coating, overcoming a significant obstacle to their neurobehavioral and sensory development research due to their aquatic nature. To understand the role of MAA in their climbing ability, researchers observed and replicated their climb using a specialized setup consisting of a tank with a light-proof lid and different surfaces for them to grasp on, over which a layer of oil was applied to diminish fluid friction's effect. It was discovered that Pacific lampreys successfully climb up vertical surfaces, but fail to adhere to smooth, non-stick surfaces, implying that MAA is essential to their ability to overcome vertical obstacles. Furthermore, when the MAA process was disabled by introducing a detergent solution, the lampreys were able to adhere to the non-stick surface, though their climbing speed significantly slowed, indicating that their climbing method involves adhering to a surface, then pulling themselves up before repeating the process. It was also observed that when the MAA process was hindered, the lampreys altered their climbing strategy, preferring to use other techniques such as using their mouth to grip small features on non-stick surfaces, rather than relying on their usual method of using their paired lateral appendages.

Recent medical research has highlighted the significance of effectively managing the immune system to prevent colon cancer progression. Through the use of immunotherapies and cancer vaccines, the immune system can be prompted to recognize and attack colon cancer cells. One method to optimize the delivery of these treatments is to create a personalized treatment plan that identifies the most effective vaccine combinations and timing to maximize the immune system's ability to detect colon cancer. A novel statistical model, specifically the Feynman-Vernon model, has been proposed to simulate the colon cancer cell elimination process based on the effectiveness of different vaccine treatments. Furthermore, a probabilistic model related to the Feynman-Verny model has been offered as an alternative to quantify the uncertainty associated with colon cancer cell elimination. Both models can be applied to any type of cancer and any form of immunotherapy, making them highly versatile.

Optimizing wireless energy efficiency in D2D systems has become a pressing research issue, given the vast potential of these systems to supplement 5G connectivity. We address this challenge by investigating energy-efficient D2D network layout design, focusing on minimizing age of information (AoI) and thereby maximizing network stability. Our approach is unique in that it differs from traditional wireless optimization methods, which typically rely on steady-state data. Initially, a mix of deep learning neural networks and classical methods are used to derive accurate AoI age predictions for individual D2D links. Subsequently, a sequential decision-making process is implemented to optimize the network layout. Our proposed method is exemplified through simulations using a residential area example, where the results demonstrate its effectiveness in controlling the AoI growth and optimizing D2D network efficiency.

To date, Euler's equations for compressible fluids have not been directly proven to conserve helicity. Although conservation of mass, momentum, and energy have been mathematically proven, determining whether helicity is preserved has been a complex problem. Building upon earlier research that extended Bernoulli's theorem to barotropic flows by introducing a key inequality, the current paper develops this idea to demonstrate that helicity is preserved in barotropic fluids. The primary advantage of this approach is the elimination of restrictive assumptions previously applied in relevant studies.

For the Davey-Stewartson II equations, the reflection coefficient of a specific nonlinear Schrödinger equation derived from multiconfocal nonlinear Schrödinger equations has been calculated, and its behavior, particularly at large values of $k$, has been examined. This investigation draws on the newly developed large-$|k|$ approach and reveals an unexpected feature: the presence of a singular point within the reflection coefficient's logarithmic derivative. As a result, the reflection coefficient does not follow the expected large-$|k|$ behavior. Instead, its real and imaginary parts exhibit distinct large-$|k|$ limits, which cannot be directly combined to yield a singular answer. Consequently, the large-$|k|$ approximation fails to yield a singular answer.

Calculations involving the orbital dynamics of binary black hole systems, using a refined theory beyond Newton's law, predict a slight irregularity in their orbits at the moment of merger. A novel approach allows for a precise prediction of this irregularity when detected through gravitational waves, using a simplified mathematical framework based on their initial conditions and the gravitational wave signal's frequency. A specific function, previously identified, is significantly altered by these initial conditions, leading to differences of up to 30% when compared to previous estimates. Furthermore, accounting for a previously overlooked effect in the binary's orbital behavior could lead to measurable irregularities in all but the most unequal masses of the binary.

Recent breakthroughs in X-ray laser technology opened doors for multiple scientific applications and drove innovation in many areas, including nonlinear X-ray physics and biological structure analysis at the atomic level. A newly developed X-ray amplifier, which uses a combination of a free-electron laser oscillator and a high-intensity x-ray amplifier, has shown the possibility of achieving high levels of coherence and intensity in the x-ray range for a prolonged period of time. The feasibility of this x-ray amplifier was evaluated using the FEECAT simulation code and the results showed that it is possible to maintain extremely high levels of coherence and intensity in the x-ray range for several milliseconds while exploring parameters of a real-world system at the DESY Hamburg facility. The success of this x-ray amplifier provides a foundation for applications such as high-intensity x-ray sources, high-energy density matter creation, and x-ray free-electron lasers with a high level of coherence and intensity.

In various network-related analyses, a dynamic graph can be utilized where-ed nodes and edges are time-wise introduced, removed, or modified, offering a more accurate representation of certain phenomena, such as internet connections or traffic patterns. This research focuses on developing an efficient algorithm for detecting unusual incidents on temporal graphs using a data structure called the spike-tree. By recording the initial occurrence of edge formations and the shortest period for edge formations, the spike-tree provides a compact representation. Then, the incident detection task is performed by analyzing the properties of the spike-tree and calculating the incident incidence rate, where an incident is defined as a edge formation that exceeds a specified threshold. This algorithm reaches a time complexity of O(M log N + M + P) where the number of nodes N, the number of edges M, and the number of incidents P are part of the input data. Moreover, experiments have been conducted using real-world data sets, demonstrating that the algorithm exhibits linear scalability in practice.

The equation set comprising the Euler equations for a perfect gas in a decreasing density medium, with initial conditions featuring an imploding shock wave, is being examined. It's established that in cases where the density decreases at a power law rates and the shock waves collapse in a spherically symmetric manner, solutions can be represented as self-similar solutions. When the adiabatic constant is greater than 1.5, a forward traveling shock wave develops, whereas for lower values of the adiabatic constant, an expanding shock wave occurs. Conversely, when the density exponent is negative but not as low as -1.5, a collapsing shock wave forms; in situations where the density exponent is greater than -1.5, a expanding shock wave develops.

Artifical Intelligence methods now incorporate explainability requirements in order to build trust with users. Nevertheless, there isn't a standardized method for crafting these requirements, which poses a challenge for engineers. The SEIRE workshop provided a platform for researchers and industry professionals to share their knowledge on integrating RE principles with software engineering. A key discussion topic involved using RE principles to foster a user-centric approach for specifying explainability needs. This approach positions the user at the center of requirements formulation, unlike AI development methodologies which often overlook this aspect.

Characterizing colorectal polyps histopathologically is crucial to personalize patient treatment and follow-up, ultimately reducing the risk of undetected invasive carcinomas. The process of polyp characterization involves examining tissue samples for signs of cancer using histological analysis. Recent advancements in deep learning have significantly improved medical pattern recognition accuracy, prompting an increased need for high-quality, annotated datasets. In response, we've developed UniToPatho, an extensive dataset consisting of 9533 annotated H&E stained patches derived from 292 whole-slide images, designed for deep learning-based training. Comprising 2870 adenomas, 1870 hyperplastic polyps, and 1512 serrated polyps, this dataset provides a robust foundation for developing effective methods to automatically identify and classify these lesions. Notably, we've also incorporated guidance from six experienced pathologists to refine the training of deep learning models and enhance accuracy, outperforming baseline models.

The issue of data leakage arises when a portion of a compressed message inadvertently falls into the opposing party's hands. This paper approaches the problem from a coding theory standpoint, focusing on the linear version of data leakage where both the compressor and expander employ linear transformations. We represent the problem as a graph-based model, in which nodes represent variables and edges signify conditional dependencies. This graphical structure aids in determining the maximum amount of leaked information and also helps us assess the effectiveness of expanded codes in preventing data leakage. Furthermore, we investigate the data leakage capabilities of specific code pairs, such as Gaussian sources and ergodic sources, and provide examples of optimal codes in these cases. To expand on the existing literature, we consider the complex version of data leakage, in which non-linear expansions are involved. However, this version introduces additional complexities that prevent us from developing a comprehensive graph-based model. As such, we must rely on general proofs. Additionally, we explore the data leakage capabilities of specific complex code pairs, such as Gaussian sources and ergodic sources, by utilizing an alternative method. We also investigate the trade-offs between the expanded code size, data leakage rate, and overall compression ratio. Finally, we propose a new metric, denoted as ARL, to assess the effectiveness of zero-error source coding in the presence of data leakage.

Deep learning-enabled integral surveillance systems are increasingly relying on bi-static synthetic aperture radar (SAR) imaging. However, RAW SAR images often require image restoration before being used, which involves addressing issues like speckle noise, shadowing, and limited data availability due to a limited number of transmitting and receiving platforms. Applying traditional noise reduction techniques directly to RAW SAR images leads to a loss of details, while data-driven approaches often struggle to produce satisfactory results on scarce and inconsistent data. To overcome these challenges, we propose an advanced generative prior model named hierarchical deep generative prior (HGDP) for SAR image enhancement by combining two interconnected components: a low-resolution feature extractor and a high-resolution generator. The efficiency of HGDP is validated through comparative experiments on various RAW SAR imaging datasets, which demonstrate its superiority over existing state-of-the-art methods.

A Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm variant incorporates quantum mechanics into a classical optimization framework. To mitigate the challenge of determining optimal quantum circuit and coefficient values, researchers have developed various methods for tuning these parameters. This study presents a novel Bayesian tuning approach, employing Bayesian optimization to selectively query an quantum simulator, leading to significant performance enhancements in various application domains, including max-cut problem, the Circuit quantum dynamics problem, and the quantum distribution estimation challenge. This method surpasses first-generation Bayesian tuning and QAOA optimization results in nearly all cases.

In various geometric and engineering applications, calculating areas of specific shapes is essential for further analysis or solution implementation. As a fundamental step in assessing the feasibility of laser scanning technology in mobile robotics and a starting point for investigating the direct approach to calculating ellipse intersection areas, this work examines methods for determining the area of the intersection of two ellipses. After evaluating potential formulas based on their suitability for numerical computation, numerical integration, and analytical derivation, this study derives a simplified expression for the area of intersection between two general ellipses in a Cartesian coordinate system. Additionally, numerical results validating the proposed formula and analyzing its computational efficiency are presented.

Building upon continuous-time model checking, which has its roots in the late 90s, a new variation called continuous duration model checking has emerged, facilitating the description of systems through (temporally ordered) sets of execution times. Despite its promising prospects, this concept remains largely underdeveloped in the literature, lacking essential tools for high-performance model checking. In an effort to bridge this gap, we integrate a specific type of reinforcement learning called q-learning into duration model checking, which until now has not been explored in existing research. This integration allows an agent to learn how to optimize a reward function by navigating a state transition graph in a dynamic environment, all within a continuous-time context. As far as we know, this marks the first instance of q-learning being applied in duration model checking; our approach is likely universally applicable to any scenario where reinforcement learning and duration models converge.

Quantum magnets' dynamical structure factor is a critical measurement, but making predictions for multi-dimensional models like Hubbard is complicated due to computational and theoretical constraints. We investigated magnetic excitations of the Hubbard model on a triangular lattice with longer-range hopping. Beginning with the 120-degree and striped patterns of magnetism, we used the self-consistent random phase approximation to determine magnon frequencies. We discovered a correlation in the striped phase related to a long-standing theoretical issue from the analogous Heisenberg model, where quantum fluctuations stabilize this pattern. We were able to outline the entire phase diagram using this new understanding and our results surprisingly matched recent numerical research. We also extended our approach to the entire Fermi surface and found that quantum fluctuations consistently modify the phase boundaries, with these changes most pronounced in the region with "order-by-disorder" effects.

Accurate vertebrae localization and identification are crucial in various medical applications related to spine disorder diagnosis and surgical planning. However, certain pathological variations (e.g., vertebral compression fractures, scoliosis, and vertebral fixation) or imaging conditions (e.g., limited visibility and metallic streak artifacts in CT scans) can make this task quite challenging. To address these difficulties, this paper presents an advanced and automated method for identifying and localizing all vertebrae in CT scans, regardless of their condition or the presence of spinal disorders. By employing a novel spine alignment technique, it ensures accurate vertebrae localization and identification. Building upon this, it formulates an optimization problem to determine the optimal position, orientation, and order of the vertebrae in the CT volume. An efficient solution to this problem is also proposed. To validate the effectiveness of the suggested approach, experimental results on a dataset of 287 CT scans with 955 pathological variations demonstrate its superior performance compared to the state-of-the-art methods, taking into account factors like vertebrae non-uniformity, artificial artifacts, and varying spinal disorders.

Stochastic thermodynamics leverages individual particle trajectories to define and analyze thermodynamic parameters. The current studies focus on the variability of key thermodynamic parameters, such as the rate of energy conversion, that are essential for assessing thermal machine efficiency and efficiency limits. To address this, we developed a general approach applied to both Markovian and non-Markovian systems, including those with multiple active reaction paths. Our framework is based on the statistical methodology of counting process subsampling, by which the random fluctuations of any process-related count can be characterized. This involves deriving the universal limiting behavior of the fluctuating cumulant series for the rate of flows and energy conversion. To achieve this, we employed a novel combination of stochastic process tools, including the addition of a suitable version of the Laplace transform inversions. Importantly, our results are presented in a form that is independent of any specific model or dynamics and are applicable to both stationary and non-stationary conditions. This involves expressing the results in terms of the system's underlying spectral densities and time-dependent transition probabilities. Our findings include precise mathematical expressions for the spectrally-resolved speed distributions, energy conversion spectra, and other limiting statistical quantities relevant to stochastic thermodynamics. These expressions are accompanied by analytical proofs of their universality and a comprehensive examination of their applicability to a diverse range of stochastic processes, including those driven by random forces, inter alia.

This research extends the concept of relative quantum field theory to any point in a projective line cut into segments by rational transformation. It achieves this by developing the theoretical framework within the context of topological field theory, specifically by utilizing FR-regular sequences to divide divisor bundles into FR-modules, and showing that these modules maintain their structure under birational transformation. By applying this framework, we analyze the behavior of relative quantum cohomology and derive evidence suggesting its singular points are determined by a simple formula in the context of genus-one curves. Additionally, we demonstrate that relative quantum field theory is invariant under birational transformation, and apply these findings to examine the properties of "extremal" cluster algebras and their mutations, also explaining the connections between relative duality, the duality of cluster variables, and the relationships between the points of their spectra.

The principle of Rayleigh's principle underpins a broad range of phenomena, including ultrasonic wave focusing and energy consolidation, which are frequently controlled using electomechanical interactions in piezoelectric materials. Nonetheless, the majority of research has concentrated on applications featuring substantial distance between the piezoelectric elements. In this research, we explore a novel scenario in which two closely spaced piezoelectric ceramics, connected by an electric circuit, completely transmit acoustic waves. This is attributed to a mutually induced polarization effect and can be mathematically described by a simplified model that generates polariton states. The theoretical model generated results align with experimental findings, demonstrating promise for innovative biomedical technologies and expanded applications in medical imaging.

We explore the use of exciton-polariton condensates in photonic integrated circuits, leveraging the unique properties of polaritons, such as superfluidity, to create versatile microsources that can function across multiple wavelengths. By incorporating microcavity design and active gain materials into the circuit, we can develop essential building blocks for photonics, including efficient emitters, all-optical switches, and optical amplifiers. Additionally, our study reveals that polariton-based sources can offer significant benefits over traditional laser sources, achieving lower power consumption, reduced thermal load, and faster switching speeds.

The disintegrating exoplanet K2-22b exhibits behaviors that vary greatly depending on time, possibly indicating massive dust storms or a unique environment. To better comprehend its atmosphere, researchers analyzed observations of the planet's transmission spectra, leveraging the Large Binocular Telescope to detect subtle changes in its stellar light. These changes reveal the presence of large particles, likely in the form of dust, and provide insight into various chemical compositions, including silicon and oxygen, which suggest the planet's surface is eroded, exposing rock and metal to its atmosphere. Annual variations in its appearance are caused by storms, while seasonal changes may be influenced by the distance from its star, which could impact the formation of these dust clouds. Compared to previous studies, this work reveals a higher rate of particle degradation, which could impact our understanding of various planetary phenomena, such as the formation of solid particles in Proxima Centauri's habitable zone or the creation of rocky particles around other terrestrial planets.

We establish a novel criterion, grounded in coherence of the Milnor algebra, to determine the feasibility of resolving the singular point on a variety through a sequence of partial desingularization. In developing this criterion, we utilize the fact that the coordinate ring of the Milnor fiber is isomorphic to a specific subring of the completion of the coordinate ring of the variety, which in turn enables us to relate the properties of the Milnor algebra to the geometric properties of the variety in question. One notable application of this criterion concerns the circumstances under which a variety can be decomposed into separate components, a question closely tied to Hilbert fundamental theorem.

Daany is an open-source, cross-platform C# library focused on data analysis and numerical computations. Designed for.NET users, it offers data manipulation and visualization tools, as well as algorithm implementations for common mathematical and statistical applications. Developed atop the NetFramework 4.5, Daany is compatible with various.NET platforms including Windows, Linux, and macOS.

I provide an in-depth analysis of Galileo's methodology, showing how his emphasis on mathematical experimentation was linked to a specific type of Platonic realism. This mathematical approach was instrumental in his scientific discoveries but led to him overlooking key issues, such as the physical implications of his own mathematical results. Galileo's innovative method, centered on using mathematics to guide experimentation, served him well in his work but ultimately prevented him from fully grasping the nature of thought and its connection to science.

The maximum probability distribution law, mirroring the Gaussian distribution's properties, can be used to model cosmic phenomena. Building on this idea, the present paper uses the Laplace distribution to study ionization processes in the early Universe, leveraging the principles of thermodynamic maximum entropy production. Our analysis reveals a significant asymmetry in the cosmic electron distribution, which is evident in the early Universe's phase of thermal equilibrium. Furthermore, we find that this asymmetry diminishes as thermal equilibrium is established. Our research demonstrates that this non-Gaussian influence has a substantial effect on ionization processes in the early Universe. Our findings also validate the widely accepted Saha model, in addition to illustrating how the Lagrange multiplier variable evolves over time with varying entropy parameters. Our study has important implications for understanding non-Gaussian phenomena in the Universe's evolution.

The analysis of magnetic reconnection, a collisionless process, necessitates complex, computationally intensive kinetic models, contrasting with more feasible fluid-based models that can still provide valuable insight into the reconnection dynamics. Our study employs the MPI-MLFF library to couple a magnetohydrodynamic solver with an ion model in this reconnection context. By adapting the embedded PIC model's domain size, resolution, and time steps, we validated its accuracy and examined how its variations impact the reconnection rates and electron and magnetic topology. Our experiments demonstrated that using the MPI-MLFF library yields notably higher magnetic reconnection rates compared to a traditional PIC model, primarily due to the substantial reduction in computation time, which can be utilized to adaptively align the embedded PIC domain with critical shock regions. As such, the MPI-MLFF framework serves as a potent tool for leveraging the strengths of both fluid and kinetic models, effectively facilitating the exploration of dynamic magnetic reconnection processes.

This research introduces Amanuensis, an innovative collaborative learning platform that facilitates mentorship between seasoned programmers and aspiring students via a sequence of hands-on software development tasks. Amanuensis was developed based on the principles of the Code Clinic, a popular BBC television program that demonstrated the utility of programming in addressing real-world issues. Amanuensis aims to bridge the gap between introductory computing lessons and in-depth software engineering education, equipping emerging professionals with the skills to tackle pressing social problems. Built utilizing Python frameworks, including Flask for web development and Django for database management, Amanuensis is an open-source tool accessible at https://amanuensis.io/. This study reports on the initial outcomes of Amanuensis, including data gathered through user feedback and usage analysis, and explores potential avenues for further research and development.
